papers.version_note: arXiv:2511.18225v2 (15 May 2026), published in Transactions on Machine Learning Research (05/2026). The file name gives the year 2025 (v1).
papers.what_it_is: A paper that argues time-varying hardware noise breaks the exchangeability of quantum conformal prediction scores, adapts Adaptive Conformal Inference to quantum models (AQCP), tests it on ibm_sherbrooke shot data and a simulator, and proves two sufficient conditions for optimal score functions.

existing.note: The guarantee is a bound on the long-run average miscoverage, carried over from Adaptive Conformal Inference (Gibbs and Candès 2021), and it is asymptotic in the number of test points. It needs the online setting: each test response must be revealed before the next prediction. The finite-sample result (Theorem 2) needs a hidden Markov chain assumption that the authors say is unlikely to hold exactly.
existing.value: The authors state AQCP provides asymptotic average coverage guarantees under arbitrary hardware noise conditions; the guarantees do not depend on exchangeability but are asymptotic in the number of test points, and AQCP assumes the response for each test point is revealed before the next test point is processed.
existing.anchor: Abstract p.1; Sections 4 and 4.1, p.8 to 9
quotes: We introduce Adaptive Quantum Conformal Prediction (AQCP), an algorithm which provides asymptotic average coverage guarantees under arbitrary hardware noise conditions.
These guarantees do not depend on exchangeability.
The trade-off for this greater generality is that the guarantees are asymptotic in the number of test points.
it assumes that the response associated with each test point is revealed before the subsequent test point is processed.
existing.certainty_reason: The asymptotic bound is quoted from Gibbs and Candès (2021), not proved in this paper.
existing.reader_inference: The bound concerns average coverage over a stream, not coverage for any single prediction.

quotes: hardware runs collected over a single day and therefore does not fully characterise longer-term drift or more structured perturbations

existing.note: The result is one processor (ibm_sherbrooke), shot data from one day, one regression task, one step size (0.03), against online QCP (QCP with an expanding calibration set). The conclusion says coverage oscillated closely around the target for both methods, and that attributing QCP's larger deviation to non-stationary noise would need further experimentation.
existing.value: On ibm_sherbrooke shot data collected on the 18th of April 2025, AQCP with γ = 0.03 showed greater stability around the target coverage than online QCP, though coverage oscillated closely around the target level for both; the authors state that attributing QCP's greater deviation to non-stationary noise would require further experimentation, since fluctuations are expected with finite samples.
